articles.title: Chilling new details of Jenny Simpson's cardiac arrest provide firsthand POV
articles.standfirst: The U.S. Olympian has shed new light on the most fateful days of her life.
articles.summary: The U.S. Olympian has shed new light on the most fateful days of her life.
articles.body:
It's not uncommon for professional athletes to undergo traumatic medical episodes, but going through a cardiac arrest is something that can truly never be seen coming - for anyone.

Jenny Simpson , a world champion distance runner who took part in the 2016 Rio Olympics , was one of the unfortunate ones who had to experience that. The Athletic recently delved deep into her episode. It happened one month ago, on June 16 , during a local event. Simpson took part in a short one-mile run with a group of eighth graders.

Everything was going normally, until she collapsed on the infield of the track following the run . Luckily for Simpson, there were physicians and physician assistants in the stands that day. Dr. Joey Pointer began administering CPR , before they were able to find an automated external defibrillator (AED) that his family had purchased for his son's track team.

Jenny Simpson was diagnosed with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy

But the AED wasn't enough to return her heart to a normal rhythm. Apparently, it wasn't a heart attack. After a few days on a ventilator, Simpson began to stabilize . And doctors found out what had gone wrong with her on that fateful day.

The Duke doctors found Simpson a whiteboard to write on, and told her she had an extremely rare genetic condition called arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, or ARVC. Like any muscle, a healthy heart suffers damage and repairs itself each time it is stressed. In people with ARVC, however, scar tissue from that stress can’t conduct electricity properly. That makes them more vulnerable to cardiac misfires, where electricity shoots in the wrong direction and causes an arrhythmia. In many cases, their hearts also thicken beyond normal.

Unfortunately, Simpson won't be able to run again . It's simply too risky given her condition, especially now that she's living " with a pacemaker and an implanted defibrillator that will shock her if she has trouble ". She can feel "the box in her chest every morning and is reminded of her ordeal" .

The silver lining, obviously, is that Simpson is alive. If it weren't for those who were in the right place at the right time on the day disaster struck, that wouldn't be the case.

articles.title: Marvin Bracy-Williams arrested for drunk driving... following his doping scandal
articles.standfirst: Sprinter’s DUI arrest adds another setback following turbulent year
articles.summary: Sprinter’s DUI arrest adds another setback following turbulent year
articles.body:
American sprinter Marvin Bracy-Williams has been arrested in Florida on suspicion of driving under the influence, adding another troubling chapter to a year that’s already brought major setbacks for the former Olympic semifinalist.

According to court documents cited by TMZ Sports and other reports, Bracy-Williams was arrested on August 3 in Orlando. Officers reportedly arrived while a tow truck was attempting to remove his vehicle from a ditch.

The tow truck driver allegedly found the 32-year-old asleep behind the wheel, with the engine running and the vehicle still in gear.

The driver reportedly contacted his employer and requested police assistance after becoming concerned that Bracy-Williams was intoxicated.

Officers subsequently reported smelling alcohol on him and said he performed poorly during field sobriety testing. He was then taken into custody on the DUI allegation. An arrest, however, doesn’t establish guilt, and the case remains a legal matter.

The arrest comes only weeks after Bracy-Williams received his latest anti-doping sanction, which has effectively brought his track career to a standstill.

A career overshadowed by doping controversy

In June, the U.S. Anti-Doping Agency announced a 12-year period of ineligibility for Bracy-Williams , his third anti-doping rule violation.

The latest sanction followed three whereabouts violations recorded between July 2025 and April 2026. USADA said the lengthy punishment reflected the fact that it was his third violation.

That penalty followed an earlier three-year, nine-month suspension tied to testosterone use, attempted tampering and whereabouts violations.

The sanction had been backdated to February 2024. USADA said Bracy-Williams had attempted to interfere with its investigation before later cooperating with authorities.

His case also became connected to a federal investigation involving Paul Askew , who was accused of supplying prohibited performance-enhancing drugs. Askew was later federally indicted and pleaded guilty under the Rodchenkov Anti-Doping Act, according to USADA.

While serving his suspension, Bracy-Williams joined the Enhanced Games, an event that openly permits athletes to use performance-enhancing substances that are banned under traditional anti-doping rules.

He competed at the inaugural event in Las Vegas in May and finished third in the 100-meter sprint.

Bracy-Williams subsequently notified USADA on June 5 that he intended to retire. The agency said his period of ineligibility would continue indefinitely unless he returned from retirement and served the remainder of his sanction. It also ruled that his competitive results from April 1, 2026 onward were disqualified, including any medals, points and prize money.

Before his recent controversies, Bracy-Williams had established himself as a notable American sprinter. He reached the 100-meter semifinals at the 2016 Olympics in Rio de Janeiro and enjoyed his biggest international success six years later.

At the 2022 World Athletics Championships, he won silver in the individual 100 meters and helped the United States secure another silver in the 4×100-meter relay. He also recorded a personal-best 9.85 seconds in the 100 meters that season.

Bracy-Williams had previously explored professional football, spending time with the Indianapolis Colts and Seattle Seahawks before playing for the Orlando Apollos in the Alliance of American Football.
